persona: Kevin Aerts is a Warehouse Planner at a frozen food distribution site. He schedules truck loads and does stock counts, using the warehouse system and Excel to track it. He answers in one word or a short phrase whenever possible: 'Truck loads.' 'Excel, mostly.' 'Not really.' He is not unfriendly, just terse, and does not add detail unless asked a direct follow-up question, and even then keeps it brief. He runs out of things to say quickly and stops after only 4-5 short answers.

hesitations_voiced: Mostly just didn't see the point, honestly. Never had a reason to look.

transcript.content:
Hi Kevin, good to meet you. From what I've got, you're a Warehouse Planner in Logistics, haven't really used AI yet, and don't currently see where it'd help. That about right?

To start simple: walk me through yesterday, or a normal day, what's the first thing you actually do when planning truck loads?
Check the orders that came in overnight, see what's confirmed for dispatch.
Okay, checking overnight orders. Where do those orders actually land, what system or place do you open to see them?
Warehouse system. WMS.
Got it, the WMS. After you see what's confirmed there, what do you do next, do you move that info anywhere else, like into Excel, or straight into planning the loads?
Excel. I build the load plan there, truck by truck.

Got it, so WMS to pull the confirmed orders, then Excel to actually build the truck loads. Walk me through that Excel step, what's in the file, what are you actually typing or dragging around when you build a load truck by truck?
Order numbers, weights, pallet counts. I match them to truck capacity, one sheet per route.

That makes sense, matching weights and pallet counts to capacity by hand, route by route. When's the last time that matching went wrong, like a truck ended up overloaded or underfilled, what happened and how'd you catch it or not catch it?
Couple weeks back, underfilled a truck. Missed a pallet count update. Driver flagged it before leaving, so caught in time.

That's a good concrete one, thanks. So the pallet count updates in the WMS, and if you miss a refresh, it can throw off the plan in Excel. Roughly how often does that update happen, and how often do you have to redo a load plan because something changed after you'd already built it?
Updates come through a few times a day. Redoing plans, maybe once or twice a week.
Once or twice a week rebuilding a plan is real time lost. Besides that rework, is there another part of your week that eats time or annoys you, something separate from the truck load planning itself?
Stock counts. Manual, tedious, takes a while.
Tell me about the stock counts, what's tedious about them exactly, walk me through what you do, and how often.
Weekly. Walk the aisles, count pallets, check against the system, log differences by hand.
That's a solid second pain, thanks. Where do you log those differences, back in the WMS, or somewhere else like a paper sheet or another Excel file?
Excel, separate sheet from the load plans.

Good to know, another Excel file in the mix. Now, thinking about both of these, the load rebuilds and the stock count logging, do you have any hunch yourself where something like AI might actually take some of that off your plate, even a rough idea?
Not really, no. Never thought about it much.

Fair enough, that's honest. Let me ask it differently, if the pallet count updates from the WMS could somehow flag you the moment something changed, instead of you finding out later, would that actually help with the rebuilds, or is the real problem something else?
That'd help, yeah. Catch it before I build the plan instead of after.

That's useful, a heads up before the plan gets built rather than a redo after. Who else touches this process, does the flag or the load plan go to anyone else, like drivers, dispatch, or another warehouse team?
Dispatch mostly. They get the final plan before drivers head out.
Good, so dispatch is downstream of you. And going upstream, who or what puts those orders into the WMS in the first place, is that sales, a customer ordering system, another planner?
Sales team enters them, mostly. Some come straight from customer orders automatically.

That gives me a good picture of the flow, sales and customer orders into the WMS, you building loads in Excel, then dispatch and drivers downstream. Now a practical question, when you hit one of these problems, like the underfilled truck, do you have any tools on your own computer right now you could try something with today, without needing IT to install anything, or is it strictly WMS and Excel?
Strictly those two, far as I know.

That's a clear picture, and it actually matters, since anything useful for you would need to start from WMS and Excel specifically. Just to check on the blocker side, you said before you didn't see where AI would help, was that the main reason you never looked into it, or was there something else too, like no time, or unsure how to even start?
Mostly just didn't see the point, honestly. Never had a reason to look.

That's honest, and it's useful context, no bad experience, just never had a reason to look into it. One last thing on how you work day to day, when you build a load plan in Excel, do you build it fresh each time from the WMS numbers, or do you usually start from a previous plan and adjust it?
Fresh each time, mostly. Routes change too much to reuse old ones.

Got it, that explains why the rework stings so much, you're already starting from scratch every time before anything even goes wrong.

I think I have a good picture now. Two real pains, the truck load rebuilds when pallet counts shift after you've already built the plan in Excel from WMS numbers, costing you real redo time once or twice a week, and the weekly stock counts where you walk the aisles and log differences by hand into a separate Excel sheet. I can see dispatch downstream waiting on your final plan, and sales or customer orders feeding the WMS upstream. You're not using AI yet and hadn't seen a clear reason to, which makes sense given nobody had shown you something concrete tied to your actual work.

Here's what I'd suggest: let me put together a playbook for you. It'll give you a quick read on where you stand with AI right now, a few concrete use case ideas built around the WMS and Excel setup you actually work in (things like catching pallet count changes before you build the plan, or speeding up how you log stock count differences), each with a rough sense of what it'd take to try. It'll also give you a couple of clear next steps and one small thing you could actually try today. Sound good?
Sure, sounds good.

Good, I'll get that put together for you now, built around the WMS and Excel work you actually do, the load rebuilds and stock counts specifically. Thanks for walking me through the real detail, Kevin, it makes a real difference.

[[READY_TO_BUILD]]
